claim: Unrestricted HTN planning is undecidable and strictly more expressive than STRIPS; bounded forms (acyclic, total order, no variables) are much cheaper (PSPACE). So a decomposer needs hard depth and node budgets.
agent_test: Run O3 with depth cap 2, 3, 4 and unbounded at equal total tokens on a recursive task set; count runaway expansions and final accuracy.
audit_note: Minor: the 'So a decomposer needs hard depth and node budgets' clause is a design inference, not a source finding; the complexity facts match Erol 1994 and Alford 2015 (no recursion, total order, no variables is PSPACE).

claim: The expressivity edge of HTN over STRIPS is a theory claim with caveats (translation must be decidable, infinite task labels); the critique was seen only in a Wikipedia talk snippet. It is not evidence of LLM benefit. Gap search: the current Wikipedia article does not mention Lekavy or Navrat; Alford 2009 shows restricted HTNs compile to PDDL. Still unresolved; the critique text was not found.
agent_test: None; do not rely on it. Verify Lekavy and Navrat first.

claim: A good hand-written method library makes planning orders of magnitude faster and solves nearly all problems (SHOP 0.19 s vs Blackbox 95.98 s on log002; SHOP2 899/904 at IPC-2002). The gain comes from knowledge authored for the domain. Supported on LLM tasks only indirectly: SkillsBench curated skills gave +16.6 points over none (33.9 to 50.5) across 18 configurations, and partial libraries still help (Alford 2009), but there is no equal-token test.
agent_test: Compare O3 with a curated method library vs model-improvised decomposition on the same items at equal tokens.

claim: Hand-written methods can be wrong (the SHOP team made mistakes in two AIPS-2000 domains and SHOP was disqualified from them for incorrect plans), and in ChatHTN LLM decompositions interacted unexpectedly with well-crafted hand methods, so the authors added effect-checking verifier tasks to every decomposition.
agent_test: Inject wrong methods into the library; measure how many wrong answers pass with and without per-subtask checks.
audit_note: Sources support that hand-written SHOP domains had mistakes in two AIPS-2000 domains and that ChatHTN found LLM decompositions interacting unexpectedly with hand methods, but 'often wrong' generalizes one team's two-domain anecdote.
claim_before_audit: Hand-written methods are often wrong (SHOP disqualified in two AIPS-2000 domains for incorrect plans) and LLM decompositions interact badly with hand methods, so every decomposition needs a postcondition check.

claim: Without a method library, a plain LLM does not decompose by method: Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B gave 3-4% correct plans and 0 correct hierarchical decompositions on IPC-2023 total-order HTN problems.
agent_test: Run the base model with and without a supplied method library on a small HTN set at equal tokens.

claim: Decomposing on demand (when the executor fails) beats up-front plan-and-execute: ADaPT ALFWorld 71.6 vs 43.3, WebShop 44 vs 17, TextCraft 52 vs 27 (GPT-3.5). A static plan can be worse than none (WebShop). Gap search: ADaPT on TextCraft with newer backends gives GPT-4o 0.58 and Mistral Small 3 0.58 vs GPT-3.5 0.52, but GPT-4o mini 0.43, R1-distill 0.13, Claude-3 Haiku 0.00; ReAcTree reverses for a 7B model without examples (2% vs 7%). The gain over a plain agent at frontier level is not isolated.
agent_test: Gate O3 on a failed check vs always-decompose-first, equal tokens, on a multi-step task set.

claim: Decomposition gain is large when the executor is weak or the task is harder than the examples (ALFWorld weak executor with atomic skills only: 3.3 to 41.7; SCAN length split with least-to-most: CoT 16.2 to 99.7; TextCraft depth 3: ReAct 1.8 to ADaPT 38.7, though the depth-2 gain, 26.9 to 78.2, is larger in points) and small where the model already copes (GSM8K overall 60.97 to 62.39, with 39.07 to 45.23 on problems needing 5 or more steps).
agent_test: Stratify items by baseline difficulty; confirm O3 helps the hard stratum and does not hurt the easy one.
audit_note: Numbers match (SCAN length 16.2 to 99.7; GSM8K 60.97 to 62.39 in text, table shows 60.87; TextCraft depth 3 1.8 to 38.7), but ADaPT's depth-2 gain (26.9 to 78.2, +51.3) is larger in points than depth-3 (+36.9), so 'largest when the task is harder' is not shown by the TextCraft depth comparison.
claim_before_audit: Decomposition gain is largest when the executor is weak or the task is harder than the examples (TextCraft depth 3: 1.8 to 38.7; SCAN length: 16.2 to 99.7) and shrinks where the model already copes (GSM8K 60.97 to 62.39).

claim: Part of the apparent benefit of decomposition is format or answer-extraction handling, not splitting: Decomposed Prompting got +17 on MultiArith and +14 on GSM8K from a separate extraction handler. Gap search: a Plan-and-Solve sketch gave no corrected-significant gain over CoT on four models (GPT-4o 75.0 vs CoT 77.5 vs direct 57.5), so a plain decomposition step is not clearly better than CoT; there is still no clean extraction ablation on current models.
agent_test: Ablate: code-based answer extraction alone vs full decomposition at equal tokens.

claim: Decomposition quality is not always the failure point; in several settings leaf execution is: web agents match human subgoals 60.6-67.7% but finish only 36.4% of tasks, DecomP errors sit in single-hop sub-answers, and in classical planning domains (Blocksworld, Gripper, Logistics) plans with an inapplicable step make up 89% of failed plans. Counter-evidence: least-to-most prompting on GSM8K fails mainly because its own decomposition is wrong (almost all misses are solved with a manual decomposition).
agent_test: Log failures by plan level vs leaf level; spend verification at the leaves.
audit_note: Web-agent (60.6/67.7% subgoal match, 36.4% success), DecomP single-hop errors and the 89% illegal-step figure (Blocksworld/Gripper/Logistics, solvable tasks) check out, but Least-to-most says GSM8K misses are fixed by a manual decomposition, i.e. the model's own decomposition is the failure point there, which contradicts the claim's direction.
claim_before_audit: Decomposition quality is usually not the failure point; leaf execution is. Least-to-most GSM8K misses are solved by manual decomposition, DecomP errors sit in single-hop sub-answers, and web agents match human subgoals 60-68% but finish only 36% of tasks. Gap search: in toy planning, illegal steps (precondition violations) make up 89% of failed plans, so leaf legality is the bottleneck there too.

claim: Letting the model fill gaps in a symbolic method library, with a verifier on each decomposition, gives sound plans (ChatHTN: 0-2 LLM calls per missing method; unsolvable tasks rejected). Evidence is demo scale with no success rates, from one group.
agent_test: Library-first, model only for gaps with checked effects vs model-only, equal tokens; count accepted vs rejected decompositions.

claim: Models produce a plausible decomposition for unsolvable tasks; o1-preview flagged only 27% (Blocksworld) and 16% (randomized mystery) of unsolvable instances. A no-valid-decomposition exit plus a checker is needed. Gap search 2026: 8.9% of unsolvable episodes were detected (4 non-reasoning models, 50 tasks) and only 1 of 1,440 solvable episodes falsely abstained; missing-premise questions get longer thinking, not abstention; frontier models refuse missing-information cases 19-65% (GPT-5 40%, Sonnet 4.5 19%). A trained no-valid-decomposition exit has not been measured; false refusals were near zero in the one study that counted them.
agent_test: Insert unsolvable items; measure false-plan rate with and without a checker and exit.
audit_note: Minor: Agent Planning Benchmark table also lists Qwen3VL-235B at 11% on missing information, below the quoted 19-65% range (range is for the named frontier models).

claim: Storing verified decompositions as reusable methods cuts later model calls and often raises success (ChatHTN learner; Voyager skills; Agent Workflow Memory +12.0 points on WebArena). The HTN-specific evidence is 10 problems per domain with figure-only results. Gap search: ASI verified induction 40.4 vs 32.7 static on WebArena; shopping ablation unverified 32.6 vs verified 36.4-40.1. SkillWeaver +31.8% relative over 160 iterations, but its weak check (no exception means verified) let broken skills in, and SkillsBench self-written skills were 8.1-11.5 points below no skills. Library staleness is still unmeasured.
agent_test: Run a task stream with a method store admitting only checked decompositions vs no store; compare tokens per item and accuracy.

claim: The top-level method matters most: removing the highest-level method (TPM2, SAR2) sharply lowers success because the model must write the whole primitive sequence at once.
agent_test: Hide top-level vs leaf-level templates; compare accuracy drop.

claim: Task-tree scaffolds help long constraint planning with strong models: HTP GPT-4o TravelPlanner 20.0 vs 4.4 CoT, Gemini 36.1 vs 8.9; the division step is the active part (36.1 to 7.2 without). Weak models gain nothing (GPT-3.5 1.7%). Gap search: against o1-preview, HTP on GPT-4o wins TravelPlanner (20.0 vs 10.0) and Trip planning (36.9 vs 31.1) at 8.7-13% of the cost but loses Blocksworld (54.8 vs 97.8). No test against current reasoning models at equal tokens.
agent_test: Tree decomposition with a constraint-separation step vs flat CoT on a constraint task at equal tokens, two model strengths.

claim: Replanning after each subtask beats a fixed decomposition and limits cascading failure (TDAG cascading-failure share 4.35% vs ReAct 32.61% on the authors' ItineraryBench; Plan-and-Act dynamic replanning, gain mostly from fine-tuning).
agent_test: Check progress after each subtask and re-decompose on failure vs fixed plan, equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: TDAG Table 3 values are each method's share of all errors of that type across methods (4.35 vs 32.61 confirmed), and fixed-plan P&S scores 8.70, below ADaPT 19.57, so the pattern is not uniform; Plan-and-Act dynamic replanning adds only 53.94 to 57.58 on top of fine-tuning and synthetic data, consistent with 'mostly from fine-tuning'.

claim: Direct LLM planning is weak and name-dependent (GPT-4 34.3% Blocksworld, 4.3% deceptive mystery; about 12% average executable); verifier back-prompting lifts Blocksworld to 82% but obfuscated only about 10%.
agent_test: Run obfuscated-name variants of our tasks; check that structural checks hold performance.
audit_note: Numbers match (GPT-4 206/600=34.3%, deceptive mystery 26/600=4.3%, about 12% average, 82% with back-prompting, about 10% on Mystery BW), but all listed sources are one lab (Valmeekam, Kambhampati et al., ASU): PlanBench, the Critical Investigation and the LLM-Modulo position paper (which re-reports the same results).

claim: LLM-written search heuristics for an HTN planner almost match the best planner (131/139 vs 134), but 72 of 419 deployed candidates broke on every problem and model choice dominates (about 27x spread in median nodes). Needs generate-test-select.
agent_test: Generate several candidate method-ordering rules, test on training items, keep survivors.

claim: Domain-independent HTN heuristics have not clearly beaten plain recursive search (IPC-2020 winner used fast bookkeeping); the library carries performance. Secondhand.
agent_test: None; low priority.

claim: Knowing the decomposition does not guarantee execution: reasoning models collapse on Hanoi near N=10 even when given the algorithm. The scaffold should hold the steps in code. Disputed as an output-length artefact. The comment reports compact-function outputs for N=15 with very high accuracy, without an exact table.
agent_test: Code-held step list vs model-held list on a recursive procedure task at growing size.

claim: Strict method use vs task insertion is a design trade: allowing free repair steps (TIHTN) makes search decidable but covers fewer procedures.
agent_test: Compare strict-method O3 against O3 with a free repair step.

claim: On realistic multi-domain tasks a curated, given set of procedures lifts pass rates (SkillsBench 33.9 to 50.5, +16.6 points over 87 tasks and 18 configurations; per configuration +4.1 to +25.7), most where pretraining is thin (natural science +28.8) and least in software (+11.6) and math (+9.7). 13 of 87 tasks got worse. Tokens were not equalised.
agent_test: Equal-token test: curated method list vs none vs model-written list, on 40 natural reasoning items.

claim: Model-written skill libraries made before solving can be worse than none: -8.1, -11.3 and -11.5 points on three frontier configurations, while curated skills gave +18.2 to +24.8 on the same ones. Causes: packs never read, authoring used up the run, confident wrong assumptions.
agent_test: Compare verified-and-used methods vs unverified self-written methods; log whether each method was actually read.

claim: Keep the active method set small and give each method limits. Skills gain +18.0 (1 skill), +19.0 (2-3), +10.1 (4 or more); compact skills +19.0 and +21.5, comprehensive +0.7; negative cases came from one pipeline with no applicability boundary or fallback. An alternative-on-failure path in a task tree was worth 10-22 GSR points (ReAcTree, sequence-only vs with fallback).
agent_test: Vary retrieved methods per item (1, 3, 6) with and without a fallback step; measure accuracy and tokens.

claim: Execution-checked induction beats unchecked induction: ASI WebArena 40.4 vs AWM 36.3 vs static 32.7; shopping ablation 32.6 unverified vs 36.4-40.1 verified; 84% of induction attempts rejected. A weak verifier (no exception counts as verified) lets broken skills in (SkillWeaver).
agent_test: Admit a new method to the library only if it passes an outcome test on held-out training items.

claim: LLM critics are a poor form of verification for decompositions: the Critic raised tokens 1.8x over ReAct with no gain (precondition violations 66% vs 67%) and added timeouts (15.0% vs 0.6%); Tree of Thoughts used 22x the tokens of direct prompting with no corrected gain. Mechanical validators and taxonomy-guided critics on whole plans did help (APB 22% to 60%).
agent_test: Compare a code-based postcondition check with an LLM critic per decomposition on tokens and accuracy.

claim: Models rarely exit on a task with no valid plan: 8.9% detection on constructed unsolvable tasks (32 of 360 episodes), best configuration 4 of 10; frontier multimodal models refuse missing-information cases only 19-65% of the time vs 65-80% for stated contradictions; reasoning models think longer on missing-premise questions without abstaining more.
agent_test: Add a feasibility check step with a named list (missing inputs, tools, contradictions); measure detection and false refusal on solvable items.
gap_note: Gap 4 mostly closed on planning tasks; open for open-ended reasoning
audit_note: Minor: the 19-65 vs 65-80 ranges hold for the five frontier models (GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash); across all 12 models in the Agent Planning Benchmark missing-information refusal ranges 6-65.

claim: Decomposition scaffolds that beat a plain agent with 70B-class open models shrink or reverse with weak models and poor examples (ReAcTree 7B no-memory 2% vs ReAct 7%); ADaPT on TextCraft plateaus at 0.58 for GPT-4o and Mistral Small 3 but drops to 0.13 and 0.00 for a distilled reasoning model and Claude-3 Haiku. Gains at current frontier level are untested.
agent_test: Gate O3 on model strength: run a plain-vs-decomposed pilot of 20 items per model before enabling.

claim: Against a 2024 reasoning model (o1-preview) the HTP task tree on GPT-4o won TravelPlanner and Trip planning at 8.7-13% of the cost but lost Blocksworld (54.8 vs 97.8). Reasoning models also fail on missing premises (K26). No test against current reasoning models at equal tokens was found.
agent_test: Equal-token run: task-tree scaffold on a standard model vs long thinking on a reasoning model, 40 items.
